#172866. Creating Privacy Preserving AI with Substra

Creating Privacy Preserving AI with Substra

📅 12 Apr 2023 | ⏱️ 4 min read (805 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • With the recent rise of generative techniques, machine learning is at an incredibly exciting point in its history.
  • In many domains that deal with sensitive information, such as healthcare, there often isn’t enough high quality data accessible to train these data-hungry models.
  • It has been revealed that this is where Federated Learning comes in.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

With the recent rise of generative techniques, machine learning is at an incredibly exciting point in its history. The models powering this rise require even more data to produce impactful results, and thus it’s becoming increasingly important to explore upcoming methods of ethically gathering data while ensuring that data privacy and security remain a top priority.

In many domains that deal with sensitive information, such as healthcare, there often isn’t enough high quality data accessible to train these data-hungry models. Datasets are siloed in different academic centers and medical institutions and are difficult to share openly due to privacy concerns about patient and proprietary information. Regulations that protect patient data such as HIPAA are essential to safeguard individuals’ private health information, but they can limit the progress of machine learning research as data scientists can’t access the volume of data required to effectively train their models. Technologies that work alongside existing regulations by proactively protecting patient data will be crucial to unlocking these silos and accelerating the pace of machine learning research and deployment in these domains.

It has been revealed that this is where Federated Learning comes in. Check out the space we’ve created with Substra to learn more!

According to recent reports, federated learning (FL) is a decentralized machine learning technique that allows you to train models using multiple data providers. Instead of gathering data from all sources on a single server, data can remain on a local server as only the resulting model weights travel between servers.

As the data never leaves its source, federated learning is naturally a privacy-first approach. Not only does this technique improve data security and privacy, it also enables data scientists to build better models using data from different sources - increasing robustness and providing better representation as compared to models trained on data from a single source. This is valuable not only due to the increase in the quantity of data, but also to reduce the risk of bias due to variations of the underlying dataset, for example minor differences caused by the data capture techniques and equipment, or differences in demographic distributions of the patient population. With multiple sources of data, we can build more generalizable models that ultimately perform better in real world settings. For more information on federated learning, we recommend checking out this explanatory comic by Google.

According to recent reports, substra is an open source federated learning framework built for real world production environments. Although federated learning is a relatively fresh field and has only taken hold in the last decade, it has already enabled machine learning research to progress in ways previously unimaginable. For example, 10 competing biopharma companies that would traditionally never share data with each other set up a collaboration in the MELLODDY project by sharing the world’s largest collection of small molecules with known biochemical or cellular activity. This ultimately enabled all of the companies involved to build more accurate predictive models for drug discovery, a huge milestone in medical research.

Sources indicate that research on the capabilities of federated learning is growing rapidly but the majority of recent work has been limited to simulated environments. Real world examples and implementations still remain limited due to the difficulty of deploying and architecting federated networks. As a leading open-source platform for federated learning deployment, Substra has been battle tested in many complex security environments and IT infrastructures, and has enabled medical breakthroughs in breast cancer research.

It has been revealed that hugging Face collaborated with the folks managing Substra to create this space, which is meant to give you an idea of the real world challenges that researchers and scientists face - mainly, a lack of centralized, high quality data that is ‘ready for AI’. As you can control the distribution of these samples, you’ll be able to see how a simple model reacts to changes in data. You can then examine how a model trained with federated learning almost always performs better on validation data compared with models trained on data from a single source.

Industry observers note that although federated learning has been leading the charge, there are various other privacy enhancing technologies (PETs) such as secure enclaves and multi party computation that are enabling similar results and can be combined with federation to create multi layered privacy preserving environments. You can learn more here if you’re interested in how these are enabling collaborations in medicine.

It has been revealed that regardless of the methods used, it's vital to stay vigilant of the fact that data privacy is a right for all of us. It’s critical that we move forward in this AI boom with privacy and ethics in mind.

If you’d like to play around with Substra and implement federated learning in a project, you can check out the docs here.

Tech Report: Graph Classification with Transformers

📅 14 Apr 2023 | ⏱️ 4 min read (786 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that in the previous blog, we explored some of the theoretical aspects of machine learning on graphs.
  • Recent findings suggest that at the moment, the only graph transformer model available in Transformers is Microsoft's Graphormer, so this is the one we will use here.
  • To follow this tutorial, you need to have installed datasets and transformers (version >= 4.27.2), which you can do with pip install -U datasets transformers.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that in the previous blog, we explored some of the theoretical aspects of machine learning on graphs. This one will explore how you can do graph classification using the Transformers library. (You can also follow along by downloading the demo notebook here!).

Recent findings suggest that at the moment, the only graph transformer model available in Transformers is Microsoft's Graphormer, so this is the one we will use here. We are looking forward to seeing what other models people will use and integrate 🤗.

To follow this tutorial, you need to have installed datasets and transformers (version >= 4.27.2), which you can do with pip install -U datasets transformers.

To use graph data, you can either start from your own datasets, or use those available on the Hub. We'll focus on using already available ones, but feel free to add your datasets!

It has been revealed that loading a graph dataset from the Hub is very easy. Let's load the ogbg-mohiv dataset (a baseline from the Open Graph Benchmark by Stanford), stored in the OGB repository:.

This dataset already has three splits, train, validation, and test, and all these splits contain our 5 columns of interest (edge_index, edge_attr, y, num_nodes, node_feat), which you can see by doing print(dataset).

In a recent development, if you have other graph libraries, you can use them to plot your graphs and further inspect the dataset. For example, using PyGeometric and matplotlib:.

On the Hub, graph datasets are mostly stored as lists of graphs (using the jsonl format).

A single graph is a dictionary, and here is the expected format for our graph classification datasets:.

In a recent development, graph transformer frameworks usually apply specific preprocessing to their datasets to generate added features and properties which help the underlying learning task (classification in our case). Here, we use Graphormer's default preprocessing, which generates in/out degree information, the shortest path between node matrices, and other properties of interest for the model.

It is also possible to apply this preprocessing on the fly, in the DataCollator's parameters (by setting on_the_fly_processing to True): not all datasets are as small as ogbg-molhiv, and for large graphs, it might be too costly to store all the preprocessed data beforehand.

It has been revealed that here, we load an existing pretrained model/checkpoint and fine-tune it on our downstream task, which is a binary classification task (hence num_classes = 2). We could also fine-tune our model on regression tasks (num_classes = 1) or on multi-task classification.

Let's look at this in more detail.

Recent findings suggest that calling the from_pretrained method on our model downloads and caches the weights for us. As the number of classes (for prediction) is dataset dependent, we pass the fresh num_classes as well as ignore_mismatched_sizes alongside the model_checkpoint. This makes sure a custom classification head is created, specific to our task, hence likely different from the original decoder head.

It is also possible to create a newly introduced randomly initialized model to train from scratch, either following the known parameters of a given checkpoint or by manually choosing them.

Industry observers note that to train our model simply, we will use a Trainer. To instantiate it, we will need to define the training configuration and the evaluation metric. The most important is the TrainingArguments, which is a class that contains all the attributes to customize the training. It requires a folder name, which will be used to save the checkpoints of the model.

For graph datasets, it is particularly vital to play around with batch sizes and gradient accumulation steps to train on enough samples while avoiding out-of-memory errors.

The last argument push_to_hub allows the Trainer to push the model to the Hub regularly during training, as each saving step.

In the Trainer for graph classification, it is important to pass the specific data collator for the given graph dataset, which will convert individual graphs to batches for training.

When the model is trained, it can be saved to the hub with all the associated training artefacts using push_to_hub.

Recent findings suggest that as this model is quite massive, it takes about a day to train/fine-tune for 20 epochs on CPU (IntelCore i7). To go faster, you could use powerful GPUs and parallelization instead, by launching the code either in a Colab notebook or directly on the cluster of your choice.

Now that you know how to use transformers to train a graph classification model, we hope you will try to share your favorite graph transformer checkpoints, models, and datasets on the Hub for the rest of the community to use!

Accelerating Hugging Face Transformers with AWS Inferentia2

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that in the last five years, Transformer models [1] have become the de facto standard for many machine learning (ML) tasks, such as natural language processing (NLP), computer vision (CV), speech, and more.
  • Sources indicate that however, for all their greatness, Transformers can be challenging to deploy in production.
  • Recent findings suggest that fitting these models on a single accelerator can be quite difficult, let alone getting the high throughput and low inference latency that applications require, like conversational applications and search.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that in the last five years, Transformer models [1] have become the de facto standard for many machine learning (ML) tasks, such as natural language processing (NLP), computer vision (CV), speech, and more. Today, many data scientists and ML engineers rely on popular transformer architectures like BERT [2], RoBERTa [3], the Vision Transformer [4], or any of the 130,000+ pre-trained models available on the Hugging Face hub to solve complex business problems with state-of-the-art accuracy.

Sources indicate that however, for all their greatness, Transformers can be challenging to deploy in production. On top of the infrastructure plumbing typically associated with model deployment, which we largely solved with our Inference Endpoints service, Transformers are large models which routinely exceed the multi-gigabyte mark. Large language models (LLMs) like GPT-J-6B, Flan-T5, or Opt-30B are in the tens of gigabytes, not to mention behemoths like BLOOM, our very own LLM, which clocks in at 350 gigabytes.

Recent findings suggest that fitting these models on a single accelerator can be quite difficult, let alone getting the high throughput and low inference latency that applications require, like conversational applications and search. So far, ML experts have designed complex manual techniques to slice large models, distribute them on a cluster of accelerators, and optimize their latency. Unfortunately, this work is extremely difficult, time-consuming, and completely out of reach for many ML practitioners.

Sources indicate that at Hugging Face, we're democratizing ML and always looking to partner with companies who also believe that every developer and organization should benefit from state-of-the-art models. For this purpose, we're excited to partner with Amazon Web Services to optimize Hugging Face Transformers for AWS Inferentia 2! It’s a latest purpose-built inference accelerator that delivers unprecedented levels of throughput, latency, performance per watt, and scalability.

Recent findings suggest that AWS Inferentia2 is the next generation to Inferentia1 launched in 2019. Powered by Inferentia1, Amazon EC2 Inf1 instances delivered 25% higher throughput and 70% lower cost than comparable G5 instances based on NVIDIA A10G GPU, and with Inferentia2, AWS is pushing the envelope again.

Sources indicate that the latest Inferentia2 chip delivers a 4x throughput increase and a 10x latency reduction compared to Inferentia. Likewise, the new Amazon EC2 Inf2 instances have up to 2.6x better throughput, 8.1x lower latency, and 50% better performance per watt than comparable G5 instances. Inferentia 2 gives you the best of both worlds: cost-per-inference optimization thanks to high throughput and response time for your application thanks to low inference latency.

Sources indicate that inf2 instances are available in multiple sizes, which are equipped with between 1 to 12 Inferentia 2 chips. When several chips are present, they are interconnected by a blazing-fast direct Inferentia2 to Inferentia2 connectivity for distributed inference on large models. For example, the largest instance size, inf2.48xlarge, has 12 chips and enough memory to load a 175-billion parameter model like GPT-3 or BLOOM.

Industry observers note that thankfully none of this comes at the expense of development complexity. With optimum neuron, you don't need to slice or modify your model. Because of the native integration in AWS Neuron SDK, all it takes is a single line of code to compile your model for Inferentia 2. You can experiment in minutes! Test the performance your model could reach on Inferentia 2 and see for yourself.

Speaking of, let’s show you how several Hugging Face models run on Inferentia 2. Benchmarking time!

We evaluated some of the most popular NLP models from the Hugging Face Hub including BERT, RoBERTa, DistilBERT, and vision models like Vision Transformers.

The first benchmark compares the performance of Inferentia, Inferentia 2, and GPUs. We ran all experiments on AWS with the following instance types:.

Note: that we did not optimize the model for the GPU environment, the models were evaluated in fp32.

When it comes to benchmarking Transformer models, there are two metrics that are most adopted:.

Recent findings suggest that we looked at latency across different setups and models to understand the benefits and tradeoffs of the new Inferentia2 instance. If you want to run the benchmark yourself, we created a Github repository with all the information and scripts to do so.

Sources indicate that the benchmark confirms that the performance improvements claimed by AWS can be reproduced and validated by real use-cases and examples. On average, AWS Inferentia2 delivers 4.5x better latency than NVIDIA A10G GPUs and 4x better latency than Inferentia1 instances.

We ran 144 experiments on 6 different model architectures:.

In a recent development, in each experiment, we collected numbers for p95 latency. You can find the full details of the benchmark in this spreadsheet: HuggingFace: Benchmark Inferentia2.

Let’s highlight a few insights of the benchmark.

Recent findings suggest that here is the latency comparison for running BERT-base on each of the infrastructure setups, with a logarithmic scale for latency. It is remarkable to see how Inferentia2 outperforms all other setups by ~6x for sequence lengths up to 256.

In a recent development, here is the latency comparison for running ViT-base on the different infrastructure setups. Inferentia2 delivers 2x better latency than the NVIDIA A10G, with the potential to greatly help companies move from traditional architectures, like CNNs, to Transformers for - real-time applications.

Sources indicate that transformer models have emerged as the go-to solution for many machine learning tasks. However, deploying them in production has been challenging due to their large size and latency requirements. Thanks to AWS Inferentia2 and the collaboration between Hugging Face and AWS, developers and organizations can now leverage the benefits of state-of-the-art models without the prior need for extensive machine learning expertise. You can start testing for as low as 0.76$/h.

The initial benchmarking results are promising, and show that Inferentia2 delivers superior latency performance when compared to both Inferentia and NVIDIA A10G GPUs. This latest breakthrough promises high-quality machine learning models can be made available to a much broader audience delivering AI accessibility to everyone.

We are delighted to introduce Hugging Face’s fresh blog for Chinese speakers: hf.co/blog/zh! A committed group of volunteers has made this possible by translating our invaluable resources, including blog posts and comprehensive courses on transformers, diffusion, and reinforcement learning. This step aims to make our content accessible to the ever-growing Chinese AI community, fostering mutual learning and collaboration.

In a recent development, we want to highlight the remarkable achievements and contributions of the Chinese AI community, which has demonstrated exceptional talent and innovation. Groundbreaking advancements like HuggingGPT, ChatGLM, RWKV, ChatYuan, ModelScope text-to-video models as well as IDEA CCNL and BAAI’s contributions underscore the incredible potential within the community.

In addition, the Chinese AI community has been actively engaged in creating trendy Spaces, such as Chuanhu GPT and GPT Academy, further demonstrating its enthusiasm and creativity.

We have been collaborating with organizations such as PaddlePaddle to ensure seamless integration with Hugging Face, empowering more collaborative efforts in the realm of Machine Learning.

We are proud of our collaborative history with our Chinese collaborators, having worked together on various events that have enabled knowledge exchange and collaboration, propelling the AI community forward. Some of our collaborative efforts include:.

According to recent reports, we are excited to announce that we will continue to strengthen our ties with the Chinese AI community by fostering more collaborations and joint efforts. These initiatives will create opportunities for knowledge sharing and expertise exchange, promoting collaborative open-source machine learning across our communities, and tackling the challenges and opportunities in the field of cooperative OS ML.

Industry observers note that as we embark on this newly introduced chapter, our collaboration with the Chinese AI community will serve as a platform to bridge cultural and linguistic barriers, fostering innovation and cooperation in the AI domain. At Hugging Face, we value diverse perspectives and voices, aiming to create a welcoming and inclusive community that promotes ethical and equitable AI development.

Join us on this exciting journey, and stay tuned for more updates on our blog about Chinese community advancements and future collaborative endeavors!

Databricks ❤️ Hugging Face: up to 40% faster training and tuning of Large Language Models

📅 26 Apr 2023 | ⏱️ 3 min read (654 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Generative AI has been taking the world by storm.
  • Over the past few weeks, we’ve gotten many requests from users asking for an easier way to load their Spark dataframe into a Hugging Face dataset that can be utilized for model training or tuning.
  • Recent findings suggest that not only was this cumbersome, but it also meant that data had to be written to disk and then read in again.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Generative AI has been taking the world by storm. As the data and AI organization, we have been on this journey with the release of the open source large language model Dolly, as well as the internally crowdsourced dataset licensed for research and commercial use that we used to fine-tune it, the databricks-dolly-15k. Both the model and dataset are available on Hugging Face. We’ve learned a lot throughout this process, and today we’re excited to announce our first of many official commits to the Hugging Face codebase that allows customers to easily create a Hugging Face Dataset from an Apache Spark™ dataframe.

— Clem Delange, Hugging Face CEO.

Over the past few weeks, we’ve gotten many requests from users asking for an easier way to load their Spark dataframe into a Hugging Face dataset that can be utilized for model training or tuning. Prior to today’s release, to get data from a Spark dataframe into a Hugging Face dataset, users had to write data into Parquet files and then point the Hugging Face dataset to these files to reload them. For example:.

Recent findings suggest that not only was this cumbersome, but it also meant that data had to be written to disk and then read in again. On top of that, the data would get rematerialized once loaded back into the dataset, which eats up more resources and, therefore, more time and cost. Using this method, we saw that a relatively small (16GB) dataset took about 22 minutes to go from Spark dataframe to Parquet, and then back into the Hugging Face dataset.

With the latest Hugging Face release, we make it much simpler for people to accomplish the same task by simply calling the upcoming “from_spark” function in Datasets:.

This allows consumers to use Spark to efficiently load and transform data for training or fine-tuning a model, then easily map their Spark dataframe into a Hugging Face dataset for super simple integration into their training pipelines. This combines cost savings and speed from Spark and optimizations like memory-mapping and smart caching from Hugging Face datasets. These improvements cut down the processing time for our example 16GB dataset by more than 40%, going from 22 minutes down to only 12 minutes.

As we transition to this new AI paradigm, organizations will need to use their extremely valuable data to augment their AI models if they want to get the best performance within their specific domain. This will almost certainly require work in the form of data transformations, and doing this efficiently over large datasets is something Spark was designed to do. Integrating Spark with Hugging Face gives you the cost-effectiveness and performance of Spark while retaining the pipeline integration that Hugging Face provides.

Industry observers note that we see this release as a upcoming avenue to further contribute to the open source community, something that we believe Hugging Face does extremely well, as it has become the de facto repository for open source models and datasets. This is only the first of many contributions. We already have aims to add streaming support through Spark to make the dataset loading even faster.

In a recent development, in order to become the best platform for owners to jump into the world of AI, we’re working hard to provide the best tools to successfully train, tune, and deploy models. Not only will we continue contributing to Hugging Face, but we’ve also started releasing improvements to our other open source projects. A recent MLflow release added support for the transformers library, OpenAI integration, and Langchain support. We also announced AI Functions within Databricks SQL that lets users easily integrate OpenAI (or their own deployed models in the future) into their queries. To top it all off, we also released a PyTorch distributor for Spark to simplify distributed PyTorch training on Databricks.

This article was originally published on April 26, 2023 in Databricks's blog.

Latest Update: Running IF with 🧨 diffusers on a Free Tier Google Colab

📅 26 Apr 2023 | ⏱️ 12 min read (2305 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~12 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • TL;DR: We show how to run one of the most powerful open-source text to image models IF on a free-tier Google Colab with 🧨 diffusers.
  • You can also explore the capabilities of the model directly in the Hugging Face Space.
  • IF is a pixel-based text-to-image generation model and was released in late April 2023 by DeepFloyd.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

TL;DR: We show how to run one of the most powerful open-source text to image models IF on a free-tier Google Colab with 🧨 diffusers.

You can also explore the capabilities of the model directly in the Hugging Face Space.

Image compressed from official IF GitHub repo.

IF is a pixel-based text-to-image generation model and was released in late April 2023 by DeepFloyd. The model architecture is strongly inspired by Google's closed-sourced Imagen.

IF has two distinct advantages compared to existing text-to-image models like Stable Diffusion:.

As a result, IF is better at generating images with high-frequency details (e.g., human faces and hands) and is the first open-source image generation model that can reliably generate images with text.

The downside of operating in pixel space and using a more powerful text encoder is that IF has a significantly higher amount of parameters. T5, IF's text-to-image UNet, and IF's upscaler UNet have 4.5B, 4.3B, and 1.2B parameters respectively. Compared to Stable Diffusion 2.1's text encoder and UNet having just 400M and 900M parameters, respectively.

Sources indicate that nevertheless, it is possible to run IF on consumer hardware if one optimizes the model for low-memory usage. We will show you can do this with 🧨 diffusers in this blog post.

In 1.), we explain how to use IF for text-to-image generation, and in 2.) and 3.), we go over IF's image variation and image inpainting capabilities.

💡 Note: We are trading gains in memory by gains in speed here to make it possible to run IF in a free-tier Google Colab. If you have access to high-end GPUs such as an A100, we recommend leaving all model components on GPU for maximum speed, as done in the official IF demo.

In a recent development, 💡 Note: Some of the larger images have been compressed to load faster in the blog format. When using the official model, they should be even better quality!

IF's text generation capabilities.

Before you can use IF, you need to accept its usage conditions. To do so:.

run the login function in a Python shell.

and enter your Hugging Face Hub access token.

Sources indicate that state-of-the-art ML should not just be in the hands of an elite few. Democratizing ML means making models available to run on more than just the latest and greatest hardware.

The deep learning community has created world class tools to run resource intensive models on consumer hardware:.

Diffusers seamlessly integrates the above libraries to allow for a simple API when optimizing large models.

The free-tier Google Colab is both CPU RAM constrained (13 GB RAM) as well as GPU VRAM constrained (15 GB RAM for T4), which makes running the whole >10B IF model challenging!

Let's map out the size of IF's model components in full float32 precision:.

There is no way we can run the model in float32 as the T5 and Stage 1 UNet weights are each larger than the available CPU RAM.

In float16, the component sizes are 11GB, 8.6GB, and 1.25GB for T5, Stage1 and Stage2 UNets, respectively, which is doable for the GPU, but we're still running into CPU memory overflow errors when loading the T5 (some CPU is occupied by other processes).

Therefore, we lower the precision of T5 even more by using bitsandbytes 8bit quantization, which allows saving the T5 checkpoint with as little as 8 GB.

Now that each component fits individually into both CPU and GPU memory, we need to make sure that components have all the CPU and GPU memory for themselves when needed.

According to recent reports, diffusers supports modularly loading individual components i.e. we can load the text encoder without loading the UNet. This modular loading will ensure that we only load the component we need at a given step in the pipeline to avoid exhausting the available CPU RAM and GPU VRAM.

The free-tier Google Colab comes with around 13 GB CPU RAM:.

And an NVIDIA T4 with 15 GB VRAM:.

Some optimizations can require up-to-date versions of dependencies. If you are having problems, please double check and upgrade versions.

We will walk step by step through text-to-image generation with IF using Diffusers. We will explain briefly APIs and optimizations, but more in-depth explanations can be found in the official documentation for Diffusers, Transformers, Accelerate, and bitsandbytes.

We will load T5 using 8bit quantization. Transformers directly supports bitsandbytes through the load_in_8bit flag.

The flag variant="8bit" will download pre-quantized weights.

It has been revealed that we also use the device_map flag to allow transformers to offload model layers to the CPU or disk. Transformers significant modeling supports arbitrary device maps, which can be used to separately load model parameters directly to available devices. Passing "auto" will automatically create a device map. See the transformers docs for more information.

The Diffusers API for accessing diffusion models is the DiffusionPipeline class and its subclasses. Each instance of DiffusionPipeline is a fully self contained set of methods and models for running diffusion networks. We can override the models it uses by passing alternative instances as keyword arguments to from_pretrained.

According to recent reports, in this case, we pass None for the unet argument, so no UNet will be loaded. This allows us to run the text embedding portion of the diffusion process without loading the UNet into memory.

IF also comes with a super resolution pipeline. We will save the prompt embeddings so we can later directly pass them to the super resolution pipeline. This will allow the super resolution pipeline to be loaded without a text encoder.

Instead of an astronaut just riding a horse, let's hand them a sign as well!

and run it through the 8bit quantized T5 model:.

Recent findings suggest that once the prompt embeddings have been created. We do not need the text encoder anymore. However, it is still in memory on the GPU. We need to remove it so that we can load the UNet.

It's non-trivial to free PyTorch memory. We must garbage-collect the Python objects which point to the actual memory allocated on the GPU.

First, use the Python keyword del to delete all Python objects referencing allocated GPU memory.

Deleting the python object is not enough to free the GPU memory. Garbage collection is when the actual GPU memory is freed.

Additionally, we will call torch.cuda.empty_cache(). This method isn't strictly necessary as the cached cuda memory will be immediately available for further allocations. Emptying the cache allows us to verify in the Colab UI that the memory is available.

We'll use a helper function flush() to flush memory.

With our now available GPU memory, we can re-load the DiffusionPipeline with only the UNet to run the main diffusion process.

The variant and torch_dtype flags are used by Diffusers to download and load the weights in 16 bit floating point format.

Often, we directly pass the text prompt to DiffusionPipeline.__call__. However, we previously computed our text embeddings which we can pass instead.

It has been revealed that IF also comes with a super resolution diffusion process. Setting output_type="pt" will return raw PyTorch tensors instead of a PIL image. This way, we can keep the PyTorch tensors on GPU and pass them directly to the stage 2 super resolution pipeline.

Let's define a random generator and run the stage 1 diffusion process.

According to recent reports, let's manually convert the raw tensors to PIL and have a sneak peek at the final result. The output of stage 1 is a 64x64 image.

And again, we remove the Python pointer and free CPU and GPU memory:.

IF comes with a separate diffusion process for upscaling.

We run each diffusion process with a separate pipeline.

Sources indicate that the super resolution pipeline can be loaded with a text encoder if needed. However, we will usually have pre-computed text embeddings from the first IF pipeline. If so, load the pipeline without the text encoder.

and run it, re-using the pre-computed text embeddings.

Again we can inspect the intermediate results.

And again, we delete the Python pointer and free memory.

The second super resolution model for IF is the previously release Stability AI's x4 Upscaler.

Let's create the pipeline and load it directly on GPU with device_map="auto".

According to recent reports, 🧨 diffusers makes independently developed diffusion models easily composable as pipelines can be chained together. Here we can just take the previous PyTorch tensor output and pass it to the tage 3 pipeline as image=image.

💡 Note: The x4 Upscaler does not use T5 and has its own text encoder. Therefore, we cannot use the previously created prompt embeddings and instead must pass the original prompt.

Unlike the IF pipelines, the IF watermark will not be added by default to outputs from the Stable Diffusion x4 upscaler pipeline.

We can instead manually apply the watermark.

In a recent development, et voila! A beautiful 1024x1024 image in a free-tier Google Colab.

We have shown how 🧨 diffusers makes it easy to decompose and modularly load resource-intensive diffusion models.

💡 Note: We don't recommend using the above setup in production. 8bit quantization, manual de-allocation of model weights, and disk offloading all trade off memory for time (i.e., inference speed). This can be especially noticable if the diffusion pipeline is re-used. In production, we recommend using a 40GB A100 with all model components left on the GPU. See the official IF demo.

The same IF checkpoints can also be used for text guided image variation and inpainting. The core diffusion process is the same as text-to-image generation except the initial noised image is created from the image to be varied or inpainted.

To run image variation, load the same checkpoints with IFImg2ImgPipeline.from_pretrained() and IFImg2ImgSuperResolution.from_pretrained().

The APIs for memory optimization are all the same!

Let's free the memory from the previous section.

For image variation, we start with an initial image that we want to adapt.

In a recent development, for this section, we will adapt the famous "Slaps Roof of Car" meme. Let's download it from the internet.

The image variation pipeline take both PIL images and raw tensors. View the docstrings for more indepth documentation on expected inputs, here.

Image variation is guided by text, so we can define a prompt and encode it with T5's Text Encoder.

Again we load the text encoder into 8bit precision.

It has been revealed that for image variation, we load the checkpoint with IFImg2ImgPipeline. When using DiffusionPipeline.from_pretrained(...), checkpoints are loaded into their default pipeline. The default pipeline for the IF is the text-to-image IFPipeline. When loading checkpoints with a non-default pipeline, the pipeline must be explicitly specified.

Let's turn our salesman into an anime character.

As before, we create the text embeddings with T5.

First, remove the Python pointers.

Next, we only load the stage 1 UNet weights into the pipeline object, just like we did in the previous section.

The image variation pipeline requires both the original image and the prompt embeddings.

In a recent development, we can optionally use the strength argument to configure the amount of variation. strength directly controls the amount of noise added. Higher strength means more noise which means more variation.

Let's check the intermediate 64x64 again.

Industry observers note that looks good! We can free the memory and upscale the image again.

For super resolution, load the checkpoint with IFImg2ImgSuperResolutionPipeline and the same checkpoint as before.

💡 Note: The image variation super resolution pipeline requires the generated image as well as the original image.

In a recent development, you can also use the Stable Diffusion x4 upscaler on this image. Feel free to try it out using the code snippets in section 1.6.

In a recent development, nice! Let's free the memory and look at the final inpainting pipelines.

The IF inpainting pipeline is the same as the image variation, except only a select area of the image is denoised.

We specify the area to inpaint with an image mask.

Sources indicate that let's show off IF's amazing "letter generation" capabilities. We can replace this sign text with different slogan.

We will mask the sign so we can replace its text.

For convenience, we have pre-generated the mask and loaded it into a HF dataset.

💡 Note: You can create masks yourself by manually creating a greyscale image.

Again, we load the text encoder first.

This time, we initialize the IFInpaintingPipeline in-painting pipeline with the text encoder weights.

Alright, let's have the man advertise for more layers instead.

Having defined the prompt, we can create the prompt embeddings.

Just like before, we free the memory.

Just like before, we now load the stage 1 pipeline with only the UNet.

Now, we need to pass the input image, the mask image, and the prompt embeddings.

Let's take a look at the intermediate output.

According to recent reports, looks good! The text is pretty consistent!

Let's free the memory so we can upscale the image.

For super resolution, load the checkpoint with IFInpaintingSuperResolutionPipeline.

The inpainting super resolution pipeline requires the generated image, the original image, the mask image, and the prompt embeddings.

Let's do a final denoising run.

Nice, the model generated text without making a single spelling error!

Industry observers note that IF in 32-bit floating point precision uses 40 GB of weights in total. We showed how using only open source models and libraries, IF can be run on a free-tier Google Colab instance.

Industry observers note that the ML ecosystem benefits deeply from the sharing of open tools and open models. This notebook alone used models from DeepFloyd, StabilityAI, and Google. The libraries used -- Diffusers, Transformers, Accelerate, and bitsandbytes -- all benefit from countless contributors from different organizations.

A massive thank you to the DeepFloyd team for the creation and open sourcing of IF, and for contributing to the democratization of good machine learning 🤗.

Training a language model with 🤗 Transformers using TensorFlow and TPUs

📅 27 Apr 2023 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1552 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • TPU training is a useful skill to have: TPU pods are high-performance and extremely scalable, making it easy to train models at any scale from a few tens of millions of parameters up to truly enormous sizes: Google’s PaLM model (over 500 billion parameters!) was trained entirely on TPU pods.
  • We’ve previously written a tutorial and a Colab example showing small-scale TPU training with TensorFlow and introducing the core concepts you need to understand to get your model working on TPU.
  • As in our Colab example, we’re taking advantage of TensorFlow's very clean TPU support via XLA and TPUStrategy.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

TPU training is a useful skill to have: TPU pods are high-performance and extremely scalable, making it easy to train models at any scale from a few tens of millions of parameters up to truly enormous sizes: Google’s PaLM model (over 500 billion parameters!) was trained entirely on TPU pods.

We’ve previously written a tutorial and a Colab example showing small-scale TPU training with TensorFlow and introducing the core concepts you need to understand to get your model working on TPU. This time, we’re going to step that up another level and train a masked language model from scratch using TensorFlow and TPU, including every step from training your tokenizer and preparing your dataset through to the final model training and uploading. This is the kind of task that you’ll probably want a dedicated TPU node (or VM) for, rather than just Colab, and so that’s where we’ll focus.

As in our Colab example, we’re taking advantage of TensorFlow's very clean TPU support via XLA and TPUStrategy. We’ll also be benefiting from the fact that the majority of the TensorFlow models in 🤗 Transformers are fully XLA-compatible. So surprisingly, little work is needed to get them to run on TPU.

Unlike our Colab example, however, this example is designed to be scalable and much closer to a realistic training run -- although we only use a BERT-sized model by default, the code could be expanded to a much larger model and a much more powerful TPU pod slice by changing a few configuration options.

Recent findings suggest that why are we writing this guide now? After all, 🤗 Transformers has had support for TensorFlow for several years now. But getting those models to train on TPUs has been a major pain point for the community. This is because:.

Industry observers note that we think XLA is the future: It’s the core compiler for JAX, it has first-class support in TensorFlow, and you can even use it from PyTorch. As such, we’ve made a massive push to make our codebase XLA compatible and to remove any other roadblocks standing in the way of XLA and TPU compatibility. This means owners should be able to train most of our TensorFlow models on TPUs without hassle.

There’s also another important reason to care about TPU training right now: Recent major advances in LLMs and generative AI have created huge public interest in model training, and so it’s become incredibly hard for most people to get access to state-of-the-art GPUs. Knowing how to train on TPU gives you another path to access ultra-high-performance compute hardware, which is much more dignified than losing a bidding war for the last H100 on eBay and then ugly crying at your desk. You deserve better. And speaking from experience: Once you get comfortable with training on TPU, you might not want to go back.

We’re going to train a RoBERTa (base model) from scratch on the WikiText dataset (v1). As well as training the model, we’re also going to train the tokenizer, tokenize the data and upload it to Google Cloud Storage in TFRecord format, where it’ll be accessible for TPU training. You can find all the code in this directory. If you’re a certain kind of person, you can skip the rest of this blog post and just jump straight to the code. If you stick around, though, we’ll take a deeper look at some of the key ideas in the codebase.

It has been revealed that many of the ideas here were also mentioned in our Colab example, but we wanted to show users a full end-to-end example that puts it all together and demonstrates it in action, rather than just covering concepts at a high level. The following diagram gives you a pictorial overview of the steps involved in training a language model with 🤗 Transformers using TensorFlow and TPUs:.

Industry observers note that as mentioned, we used the WikiText dataset (v1). You can head over to the dataset page on the Hugging Face Hub to explore the dataset.

Since the dataset is already available on the Hub in a compatible format, we can easily load and interact with it using 🤗 datasets. However, for this example, since we’re also training a tokenizer from scratch, here’s what we did:.

You can find the tokenizer training code here and the tokenizer here. This script also allows you to run it with any compatible dataset from the Hub.

💡 It’s easy to use 🤗 datasets to host your text datasets. Refer to this guide to learn more.

Industry observers note that once the tokenizer is trained, we can use it on all the dataset splits (train, validation, and test in this case) and create TFRecord shards out of them. Having the data splits spread across multiple TFRecord shards helps with massively parallel processing as opposed to having each split in single TFRecord files.

It has been revealed that we tokenize the samples individually. We then take a batch of samples, concatenate them together, and split them into several chunks of a fixed size (128 in our case). We follow this strategy rather than tokenizing a batch of samples with a fixed length to avoid aggressively discarding text content (because of truncation).

We then take these tokenized samples in batches and serialize those batches as multiple TFRecord shards, where the total dataset length and individual shard size determine the number of shards. Finally, these shards are pushed to a Google Cloud Storage (GCS) bucket.

If you’re using a TPU node for training, then the data needs to be streamed from a GCS bucket since the node host memory is very small. But for TPU VMs, we can use datasets locally or even attach persistent storage to those VMs. Since TPU nodes are still quite heavily used, we based our example on using a GCS bucket for data storage.

You can see all of this in code in this script. For convenience, we have also hosted the resultant TFRecord shards in this repository on the Hub.

If you’re familiar with using 🤗 Transformers, then you already know the modeling code:.

But since we’re in the TPU territory, we need to perform this initialization under a strategy scope so that it can be distributed across the TPU workers with data-parallel training:.

Similarly, the optimizer also needs to be initialized under the same strategy scope with which the model is going to be further compiled. Going over the full training code isn’t something we want to do in this post, so we welcome you to read it here. Instead, let’s discuss another key point of — a TensorFlow-native data collator — DataCollatorForLanguageModeling.

It has been revealed that dataCollatorForLanguageModeling is responsible for masking randomly selected tokens from the input sequence and preparing the labels. By default, we return the results from these collators as NumPy arrays. However, many collators also support returning these values as TensorFlow tensors if we specify return_tensor="tf". This was crucial for our data pipeline to be compatible with TPU training.

Thankfully, TensorFlow provides seamless support for reading files from a GCS bucket:.

If args.dataset contains the gs:// identifier, TensorFlow will understand that it needs to look into a GCS bucket. Loading locally is as easy as removing the gs:// identifier. For the rest of the data pipeline-related code, you can refer to this section in the training script.

In a recent development, once the datasets have been prepared, the model and the optimizer have been initialized, and the model has been compiled, we can do the community’s favorite - model.fit(). For training, we didn’t do extensive hyperparameter tuning. We just trained it for longer with a learning rate of 1e-4. We also leveraged the PushToHubCallback for model checkpointing and syncing them with the Hub. You can find the hyperparameter details and a trained model here: https://huggingface.co/tf-tpu/roberta-base-epochs-500-no-wd.

Once the model is trained, running inference with it is as easy as:.

If there’s one thing we want to emphasize with this example, it’s that TPU training is powerful, scalable and easy. In fact, if you’re already using Transformers models with TF/Keras and streaming data from tf.data, you might be shocked at how little work it takes to move your whole training pipeline to TPU. They have a reputation as somewhat arcane, high-end, complex hardware, but they’re quite approachable, and instantiating a large pod slice is definitely easier than keeping multiple GPU servers in sync!

In a recent development, diversifying the hardware that state-of-the-art models are trained on is going to be critical in the 2020s, especially if the ongoing GPU shortage continues. We hope that this guide will give you the tools you need to power cutting-edge training runs no matter what circumstances you face.

As the great poet GPT-4 once noted:.

If you can keep your head when all around you Are losing theirs to GPU droughts, And trust your code, while others doubt you, To train on TPUs, no second thoughts;.

If you can learn from errors, and proceed, And optimize your aim to reach the sky, Yours is the path to AI mastery, And you'll prevail, my friend, as time goes by.

Sure, it’s shamelessly ripping off Rudyard Kipling and it has no idea how to pronounce “drought”, but we hope you feel inspired regardless.

#172828. Industry News: Building a Human Review Pipeline for AI Search: A Practical Developer’s Guide

📅 30 Oct 2026 • ⏱️ 11m • 📚 Deep Dive (2244 w)
📖 Baca
AI & Tech ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Sitepoint ↗ Open Full Page

Industry News: Building a Human Review Pipeline for AI Search: A Practical Developer’s Guide

📅 30 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 11 min read (2244 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sitepoint

⏱️ ~11 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Stay up to date with AI tools, model releases, and developer workflows that matter.
  • In a recent development, 7 Day Free Trial.
  • An AI search feature can return valid JSON, render correctly, and still give an unhelpful answer.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Stay up to date with AI tools, model releases, and developer workflows that matter.

Sources indicate that weekly. Free. One click to leave.

In a recent development, 7 Day Free Trial. Cancel Anytime.

An AI search feature can return valid JSON, render correctly, and still give an unhelpful answer.

Industry observers note that imagine a documentation assistant answering a question about an API's current authentication requirements. It retrieves an outdated page, summarizes it fluently, and displays a citation. Every technical component appears to work, but the user receives instructions that no longer apply.

Automated checks are valuable, yet they cannot replace a clearly defined judgment about whether an answer solves the user's problem.

This guide builds a human-review workflow for a hypothetical API documentation assistant. You will define a review rubric, validate submissions with Python, measure reviewer disagreement, and turn accepted judgments into regression cases. The Python examples use Pydantic 2 and scikit-learn; they do not require a model-provider API key.

Start by identifying the failure you want to detect.

A documentation assistant usually has several stages: receive a question, retrieve relevant documents, generate an answer, and present that answer with supporting material.

Sources indicate that do not collapse these into a single “good answer” rating. A low score without a reason tells the team little about what to fix.

SitePoint’s introduction to retrieval-augmented generation provides background on how retrieval and generation fit together.

Recent findings suggest that preserve the exact question, answer revision, retrieved passages, document versions, and retrieval timestamp for each run. Store a snapshot manifest with stable passage IDs, source URLs, and content hashes. Reviewers should see the material supplied to that run, not today’s edited page. Keep the model and prompt configuration with the run so a later review can be traced to the behavior it evaluated.

A useful rubric defines observable criteria and separates evidence support from task completion and source suitability. Give each review the same user task and expected API version. Otherwise, reviewers may judge different questions while appearing to disagree about one answer.

For an answer about API authentication, use separate labels such as:.

Supported: every material factual claim is backed by the supplied evidence.

Partially supported: some material claims lack support, while others are grounded.

Unsupported: the answer's central instruction lacks support or contradicts the evidence.

Cannot assess: the necessary evidence is missing, unreadable, or inaccessible.

Define task completion independently as complete, incomplete, or cannot assess. For source suitability, use suitable, outdated, or cannot assess. An answer can faithfully summarize an obsolete page while failing the request for current instructions.

Consider a fictional API migration: version 2 accepts X-API-Key, while version 3 requires Authorization: Bearer . If the supplied evidence contains only the version 2 page, an answer repeating X-API-Key can be supported by its evidence but still use an outdated source. If the evidence explicitly requires Bearer and the answer invents X-API-Key, label the answer unsupported. These are different engineering failures.

Also establish what reviewers should do when the source is outdated. They may correctly conclude that an answer reflects its evidence while separately flagging that evidence as unsuitable for the user's current task.

Start with a calibration batch covering clear successes, unsupported claims, missing evidence, and version mismatches. Have two reviewers label the same items independently, then compare their reasons. Revise ambiguous definitions before increasing volume; the batch is for improving the rubric, not estimating production quality.

It has been revealed that keep a rubric version on every review. Labels produced under different definitions should not be mixed without checking comparability.

A spreadsheet can help during exploration, but an engineering pipeline needs a stable record format.

Industry observers note that pydantic can validate a review record before it enters the dataset. Install Pydantic 2 and scikit-learn in your project environment, then use this model:.

from pydantic import BaseModel, ConfigDict, Field, ValidationError.

model_config = ConfigDict(extra="forbid", strict=True).

item_id: str = Field(min_length=1).

answer_revision: str = Field(min_length=1).

snapshot_id: str = Field(min_length=1).

reviewer_id: str = Field(min_length=1).

rubric_version: Literal["auth-v1"].

"supported", "partially_supported",.

completion: Literal["complete", "incomplete", "cannot_assess"].

source_fit: Literal["suitable", "outdated", "cannot_assess"].

rationale: str = Field(min_length=20, max_length=2000).

Industry observers note that strict mode limits type coercion, and extra="forbid" rejects unexpected fields. The model checks shape and allowed values; it cannot establish that a judgment is correct. A minimum rationale length does not guarantee a useful explanation. The snapshot ID references a manifest, which can also record that retrieval produced no usable passages.

It has been revealed that on the server, resolve the item, answer revision, snapshot, and passage IDs against the stored run. Reject IDs that do not belong together. Obtain the reviewer identity from the authenticated session rather than trusting a submitted reviewer_id. Store a server-generated submission time and preserve review revisions instead of silently overwriting earlier judgments.

Run this after the model definition. It accepts one fictional review and rejects both an unknown label and an extra field:.

"answer_revision": "answer-02",.

"rationale": "The answer invents X-API-Key; p1 requires Bearer.",.

review = Review.model_validate(payload).

{**payload, "support": "mostly_fine"},.

{**payload, "confidence": 0.99}.

except ValidationError as error:.

print(error.errors()[0]["type"]).

raise AssertionError("Invalid review was accepted").

The expected error types are literal_error and extra_forbidden. Add separate integration tests for mismatched evidence IDs, unauthorized submissions, and retries. Use a database uniqueness rule or an idempotency key so a repeated request does not create a second independent review.

Sources indicate that more reviews do not automatically produce better evidence. If a task is ambiguous, scaling it can simply reproduce the ambiguity.

Recent findings suggest that the workflow needs clear eligibility requirements, examples, escalation routes, and acceptance criteria. Reviewers assessing API behavior may need domain knowledge that general writing fluency does not provide.

According to recent reports, if you work with an external AI-data contributor service such as Acquirox, define the task contract before assigning work: required expertise, permitted source material, output fields, and escalation rules. Keep ownership of the rubric, evaluation set, and acceptance decisions within the product team. Contributor capacity alone does not establish expertise in the API being reviewed.

Pilot the actual task in the review interface. Track drafts, submitted reviews, items needing adjudication, and final decisions as distinct workflow states. Reviewer judgments should remain immutable once submitted; corrections should create a upcoming revision with a reason. Keep adjudication separate from the original labels.

Sources indicate that for data involving owners or contributors, document permitted uses, access boundaries, and retention. Remove credentials and unnecessary personal information from review material. An internal support transcript should not become a broadly accessible annotation task by accident.

Distinguish annotation from usability research. A skilled reviewer can judge whether an answer is supported, but that does not prove a first-time user can understand the interface.

SitePoint’s guide to choosing usability tests and participants offers related guidance on matching participants and methods to the question being investigated.

The review interface shapes the data it collects.

Label Studio is an option for configurable labeling interfaces and data import/export. If you use it, map exported annotations into the Review schema through an adapter; do not assume its export structure matches your application contract. A custom interface may be appropriate when reviewers need API-version navigation or passage-level citations.

For the documentation assistant, show:.

The original question and relevant user context.

The evidence snapshot supplied to the model.

Separate controls for support and task completion.

A rationale field and an explicit “cannot assess” option.

Display stable passage IDs beside the evidence and let reviewers attach those IDs to their rationale. Show the source version and retrieval time near each passage. Render retrieved content as untrusted text or sanitized markup, and never treat instructions embedded in a source document as reviewer instructions. Avoid loading executable third-party content inside the review panel.

Industry observers note that avoid showing a preferred model name or a previous reviewer's verdict before an independent judgment. For pairwise comparisons, randomize answer order and include appropriate tie or neither-acceptable outcomes.

Design for keyboard use, visible focus, readable text, and explicit selection states. Keep evidence and the answer accessible without requiring excessive horizontal scrolling.

Industry observers note that start all judgment controls unselected and validate them on submission. Use labeled radio groups, an accessible error summary, and visible saving/submission status. A failed save should preserve the draft. Disable duplicate submissions in the UI, but enforce duplicate handling on the server as well.

In a recent development, practical check: observe a reviewer completing several borderline examples. Record where they pause, misinterpret a label, or cannot find the necessary source material.

When two reviewers disagree, investigate before reducing their decisions to a majority vote.

Different assumptions about the user's expertise.

A genuine error by one or both reviewers.

Sources indicate that preserve independent labels and store the adjudicated result separately. This allows the team to study ambiguity instead of erasing it.

For two reviewers applying categorical labels to the same items, scikit-learn provides Cohen's kappa:.

from sklearn.metrics import cohen_kappa_score.

("q1", "a1", "s1", "auth-v1"): "supported",.

("q2", "a1", "s2", "auth-v1"): "unsupported",.

("q3", "a1", "s3", "auth-v1"): "supported",.

("q4", "a1", "s4", "auth-v1"): "partially_supported".

("q3", "a1", "s3", "auth-v1"): "partially_supported".

raise ValueError("Review sets must contain identical items").

left = [a[key] for key in keys].

right = [b[key] for key in keys].

raw_agreement = sum(x == y for x, y in zip(left, right)) / len(keys).

print(f"Raw agreement: {raw_agreement:.2f}").

print(f"Kappa: {cohen_kappa_score(left, right):.2f}").

According to recent reports, this toy example prints raw agreement of 0.75 and kappa of about 0.64. Four items are not enough to assess a review program. In production, check for duplicate reviews before building dictionaries, use one rubric version per comparison, report unmatched items, and align all records by item, answer revision, and evidence snapshot.

Industry observers note that kappa measures agreement beyond chance under its assumptions, not correctness. Inspect raw agreement, label frequencies, and the disagreement table alongside it. A single-category batch can make kappa undefined; report that limitation rather than substituting a reassuring score. Treat cannot_assess explicitly and report its frequency instead of silently excluding difficult cases.

If both reviewers apply the same flawed rubric consistently, agreement can be high while the evaluation remains unhelpful.

Once difficult cases are adjudicated, turn them into regression cases with explicit acceptance criteria. For the fictional authentication task: use version 3 evidence, cite the passage requiring Bearer, and do not invent a header. If version 3 evidence is missing, an acceptable response should explain the gap rather than provide confident instructions.

Source snapshot and document version.

Expected behavior or acceptance criteria.

Model and prompt configuration.

Review and adjudication records.

Sources indicate that DVC can track larger datasets alongside Git. In an existing Git repository with DVC initialized and data/reviewed-auth.jsonl present, a minimal versioning step is:.

dvc add data/reviewed-auth.jsonl.

git add data/reviewed-auth.jsonl.dvc data/.gitignore.

git commit -m "Version authentication review cases".

This commits metadata, not the dataset bytes. Configure an access-controlled DVC remote and push the data before expecting another machine or CI runner to retrieve it. Keep credentials and sensitive review material out of public repositories.

According to recent reports, keep development examples separate from held-out evaluation cases. If developers repeatedly tune prompts against the same questions, those questions become less useful as evidence of generalization.

Split related examples together where appropriate. Near-duplicate questions from one support conversation should not be scattered across development and evaluation sets.

Use two evaluation passes. First, hold the evidence snapshot fixed to compare answer-generation changes. Then test retrieval against the intended document versions to detect stale or irrelevant sources. Record per-item outcomes and report failures by category; an overall improvement can hide a regression in version-specific or multilingual questions.

SitePoint’s article on testing nondeterministic AI behavior provides further context for repeatable evaluation workflows.

A correct answer can still fail in the interface.

Owners may overlook a caveat, misunderstand whether an operation has been performed, or miss that the evidence applies to an older API version.

Pair answer review with practical usability tasks:.

Find the authentication requirements for version 3 and identify the source that supports them.

Observe whether consumers complete the task and whether their confidence matches the available evidence.

SitePoint’s overview of user research methods helps distinguish task observation from preference surveys.

Sources indicate that turn interface failures into browser tests: a citation opens the expected document version, its passage ID matches the displayed evidence, missing evidence offers a recovery action, and a failed review submission preserves the draft. Verify that reviewers cannot access unassigned restricted items by changing an ID in the URL. These checks complement human judgments; they do not replace them.

In a recent development, do not use a fluent response as a substitute for a clear interaction. The interface should distinguish retrieved information, generated interpretation, and actions the application has actually completed.

According to recent reports, start with one authentication task, a versioned rubric, and a small calibration batch. Use Pydantic for ingestion checks, Label Studio or a custom interface for review, scikit-learn for agreement analysis, and Git/DVC for dataset provenance. Add each tool only when it solves a concrete workflow need.

Recent findings suggest that at release time, run deterministic checks for schema, evidence references, permissions, and interface behavior. Compare candidate answers against adjudicated acceptance criteria and send upcoming ambiguous failures back for review. Record the dataset revision and configurations with the results so another developer can reproduce the comparison.

The purpose of human review is to produce evidence the team can act on. A smaller collection of well-defined, traceable judgments is often more useful than a large pile of ratings whose meaning nobody can explain.

Sooner or later someone on your team asks it. Maybe it’s a product manager, maybe the head of content, maybe a teacher who’s just marked forty near-identical essays: can we tell when people are pasting in ChatGPT output?

The short answer is no, not with certainty. Anyone who promises you that is selling something.

But you can get a useful signal, and you can show it to the people who actually make the call: editors, teachers, moderators. In this tutorial you’ll build a small Express app that takes some text, sends it to an AI detector API, waits for the result, and highlights the sentences that look machine-written.

Recent findings suggest that I’m using the Quetext AI Detector API here. It scores each sentence, not just the whole document, and you can try it without a subscription. Most detection APIs follow the same submit, poll, fetch pattern, though. If you switch providers later, you’ll rewrite one file.

Put the key in an environment variable. Don’t hard-code it, and don’t let it anywhere near the browser.

Sources indicate that you’ll make three calls. Analysis takes a few seconds, so the API hands you a ticket and makes you come back for the result. Keep the Quetext API docs open in another tab while you follow along; they list every endpoint, field and error code.

Every request sends your key in an X-API-Key header. The minimum input is 50 words, which sounds annoying until you realise no detector can say anything useful about a two-line comment.

And remember this number: 10 requests every 5 seconds, per account. Progress checks count. It’ll come back to bite you in the production section if you ignore it.

According to recent reports, create quetext.js. I like keeping everything provider-specific in one file, so the rest of the app has no idea who’s doing the detecting.

Three decisions in there that are worth a sentence each:.

In a recent development, the errors keep their HTTP status code. A 402 means you’ve run out of credit and a 429 means you’re polling too fast, and you’ll want to handle those differently from “something broke.”.

Recent findings suggest that it polls every 2.5 seconds because Quetext’s docs suggest 2 to 3. Polling faster won’t speed the report up. You’ll just burn through the rate limit.

And there’s a hard timeout. Leave it out and one stuck report can hang a request forever. That’s a miserable bug to track down at 11pm.

It has been revealed that next, server.js. It checks the input, runs the three calls, and gives the frontend a simple response that doesn’t mention Quetext anywhere.

According to recent reports, look at the mapping at the end. generated_prob becomes probability, and ai_score comes back as a string like "82.50", so it gets parsed into a number. It’s a small detail. But it means your frontend never learns which provider’s field names it’s dealing with, and that’s what makes swapping providers a one-file change.

Show someone “64% AI” and they’ll jump to a conclusion. Show them a paragraph with three sentences shaded pink and they’ll actually read it.

Industry observers note that so the page shows every sentence, coloured by how likely it is to be AI-generated. Create public/index.html:.

Run node server.js and open http://localhost:3000. Try two samples: something you wrote yourself, then a raw chatbot answer on the same topic. Seeing which sentences light up teaches you more about how these detectors work than any diagram I could draw.

Recent findings suggest that A quick security point. Those sentences came from your owners, then went through an outside service. Treat them as untrusted. That’s why the code uses textContent and never innerHTML, as the OWASP XSS prevention cheat sheet recommends.

According to recent reports, the demo keeps an HTTP request open while it polls. Fine on your laptop. Not fine with real traffic.

According to recent reports, submit the text, save the report id with a pending status, and respond straight away. A worker (BullMQ, a cron job, a serverless queue, whatever you already use) does the polling and updates the record once it’s done. The UI states “Checking…” until the result indicates up.

Here’s how it goes wrong. It’s Monday morning, 20 editors open their review queues and click “Check” at roughly the same time. Each request polls on its own, and within a few seconds you’ve hit 429s across the board, because the 10-per-5-seconds limit covers your whole account, not each user.

According to recent reports, use one worker that loops through every pending report, with a short pause between calls. Problem solved.

Industry observers note that you pay per word, so don’t check every blog comment. Article submissions, assignments and paid freelance work usually justify the cost. Cache results against a hash of the text too. Someone who submits the same draft three times shouldn’t cost you three times.

AI detection doesn’t catch copying. Someone can lift a 2019 blog post word for word and it’ll score 0% AI, because a human wrote it. Just not this human. If originality matters to your product, the same API has plagiarism endpoints that work exactly the same way. The API documentation covers both.

Recent findings suggest that developers skip this part. It’s also the part that ends up in angry support tickets.

In 2023, Liang and colleagues at Stanford ran essays written by non-native English speakers (all human, written for the TOEFL) through seven AI detectors. On average, the detectors labelled more than 61% of them as AI-generated. Simple vocabulary and textbook grammar read as “predictable,” and predictability is exactly what detectors look for.

Industry observers note that picture an international student getting an automatic zero because a script remarked so. You don’t want to be the person who built that.

Do that and the detector is a fast first pass that points people at what’s worth a closer look. Your humans still make the call.

Industry observers note that you send text, the service checks how predictable each sentence would be to a language model, and you get back a probability that a machine wrote it. Most of these APIs are asynchronous. You submit, get a report ID, poll until it’s ready, then fetch the result. The better ones score individual sentences as well as the whole text, which makes building a sensible review screen much easier.

Sources indicate that more than you’d think. Quetext’s API won’t accept fewer than 50 words, and in practice scores settle down once you’re past about 300. A product title or a one-line comment just doesn’t give a detector enough to go on. For short content, either group related pieces together or don’t bother checking it.

No. Detectors make mistakes, and research indicates they flag non-native English writers far more often than native speakers. Use the score to decide what a human looks at first, not to block anything. Give reviewers the highlighted sentences, give people a way to explain themselves, and log what you decided. Your users get treated fairly and your support team avoids a pile of angry tickets.

In a recent development, poll at the speed the provider recommends (every 2 to 3 seconds for Quetext), and remember that those polls count against your limit too. Once you’re in production, move checks into a background queue and let one worker poll every pending report, rather than having each user request poll by itself. When you do get a 429, wait a moment and retry.

No. If the browser calls the API directly, your key ends up in the frontend code where anyone can copy it and spend your credit. Keep the key in an environment variable on your server and send requests through your own endpoint, like the one in this tutorial. That also gives you somewhere to check input length, apply per-user limits and cache results before you pay for anything.
